Learning Objectives
Discuss the advantages and disadvantages of autografts and allografts.
Explain how to choose an appropriate graft based on patient age and activity level.
Review the basic biomechanical properties of implants available for sports medicine
procedures.
Describe the common modes of failure with various types of implants.
Introduction
Soft-tissue grafts are commonly used in sports medicine for ligament or tendon reconstruction
(anterior cruciate ligament [ACL] reconstruction being the most common) or are used to

Graft options include autografts, allografts, synthetic grafts, and xenografts.
The strengths and weaknesses associated with different autografts and allografts are
important to understand.
Graft options and their associated strengths and weaknesses should be discussed with the
patient preoperatively because the selected tissue type may affect the postoperative
rehabilitation process.
Graft Options for ACL Reconstruction
Multiple graft options are available for ACL reconstruction, each of which is associated with
advantages and disadvantages.
Autografts are harvested from the patient— and are the most common type of graft for ACL
reconstruction in young and high-performance athletes. Common autografts include bone-
patellar tendon-bone (BPTB), hamstring, and quadriceps tendons.
Advantages: using the patient’s own tissue, improved graft viability/longevity
Disadvantages: donor site morbidity and increased surgical time attributed to graft harvest
Allografts are obtained from cadaver model specimens. Typical allografts include patellar,
hamstring, quadriceps, Achilles, and tibialis anterior/posterior tendons.
Advantages: decreased complications related to donor-site morbidity, decreased surgical
time, smaller incisions, improved cosmesis, and decreased postoperative pain
Disadvantages: increased failure rate, variable tissue quality, risk of viral or bacterial disease
transmission.
Scaffolds are used to augment tendon repairs, such as patellar tendon repair and Achilles
tendon repair. Common scaffolds include xenografts, which are derived from animal tissue;
acellular human dermal allografts; and other synthetic materials.

Graft Options for ACL Reconstruction
Autografts are grafts harvested from the patient and are the most common type of graft
for ACL reconstruction in young and high-performance athletes. The most common
types of autografts include BPTB, hamstring, and quadriceps tendon. The disadvantages
of autografts are longer surgical time and donor site morbidity. Although BPTB is the

BPTB Autograft

BPTB Autograft
BPTB autograft consists of the middle third of the patellar tendon harvested with
adjacent bone from the inferior pole of the patella and the proximal tibia (Figure 1). The
inclusion of bone plugs at both ends of the graft is thought to provide faster
incorporation compared with other soft-tissue graft types.1 Studies have shown low
failure rates and high patient satisfaction, particularly in patients who desire to return to
high-level sports activity. A recent metanalysis reviewed 2,348 athletes and found that
those who underwent ACL reconstruction with the use of BPTB had a 10.4% higher
overall rate of return to sports activity compared with those who underwent ACL
reconstruction with the use of hamstring tendon (81% versus 70.6%). In addition, those
treated with the use of BPTB had a slightly higher rate of return to preinjury level of
performance (50% versus 48.5%) and a slightly lower re-rupture rate (2.2% versus 2.5%)
compared with the hamstring group.2
Complications associated with BPTB autograft include anterior knee pain, kneeling pain,
patellar fracture, patellofemoral crepitus, patellar tendon rupture, extension loss, and
increased rates of postoperative osteoarthritis. The most common postoperative
complications after use of BPTB autograft are anterior knee pain, kneeling pain, and
extension loss. A metanalysis of 21 studies showed that, compared with hamstring
autograft, BPTB autograft was associated with a substantially lower rate of graft failure,
and a considerably greater proportion of patients had a side-to-side difference of less
than 3 mm on KT-1000 arthrometer testing. However, compared with the hamstring
group, the BPTB group had a substantially higher rate of manipulation under anesthesia
(6.3% versus 3.3%) and anterior knee pain (17.4% versus 11.5%).3 Another study
comparing BPTB and hamstring autograft found that a considerably higher number of
patients in the BPTB group experienced anterior knee pain (36% versus 12%) and
kneeling pain (72% versus 44%) at 5-year follow-up.4

Hamstring Tendon Autograft

Hamstring Tendon Autograft
Hamstring tendon autograft consists of harvesting the patient’s ipsilateral
semitendinosus and/or gracilis at the site of insertion on the tibia. The tendons can be
harvested via an anteromedial incision, and the same incision can be used to drill the
tibial tunnel during ACL reconstruction. Biomechanical studies have shown that
quadruple hamstring tendon grafts have greater strength and stiffness than BPTB
autografts.
Disadvantages of hamstring tendon autografts include graft harvest morbidity, which
may result in sore hamstrings and decreased knee flexion strength, particularly at higher
flexion angles. Considerable knee flexion deficit was found as long as 24 months
postoperatively in a study comparing hamstring tendon autograft with BPTB autograft.1
Patients undergoing ACL reconstruction with the use of hamstring autograft typically
follow a more conservative postoperative protocol because the soft-tissue graft requires
more time for biologic healing and integration into the bone tunnels as a result of the

lack of an associated bone plug. Soft-tissue grafts have been reported to incorporate
into bone within 8 to 12 weeks postoperatively. This time frame is approximately 2 to 6
weeks longer than the time frame for grafts containing bone.5 In addition, analysis of
data from the Multicenter Orthopaedic Outcomes Network Knee Group has shown an
increased risk of infection with the use of hamstring autografts compared with BPTB
autografts (odds ratio, 4.6; P = 0.026).6
Quadriceps Autografts

Quadriceps Autografts
Quadriceps autografts are less commonly used but recently have been gaining
popularity. This graft is harvested from the patient’s ipsilateral knee via an anterior
approach proximal to the patella (Figure 2). A systematic review of 14 studies found
quadriceps tendon autografts to be a safe and reproducible graft choice for ACL
reconstruction.7 In a study comparing quadriceps and hamstring autografts, patients
treated via quadriceps autograft had similar knee stability and functional outcomes
postoperatively while having better outcomes in knee flexion strength.8
Donor site morbidity after quadriceps tendon autograft harvest includes hematoma
formation, cosmetic deformity if the graft is harvested too proximally into the rectus
myofascial junction, and patellar fracture; however, studies have shown similar
functional and objective outcomes and failure rates between quadriceps tendon and
BPTB and hamstring tendon autografts with less donor site morbidity, such as a lower
incidence of anterior knee and kneeling pain compared with BPTB and considerably
lower flexion strength loss compared with hamstring tendon autografts.8-12 In addition,
the risk of iatrogenic injury to the infrapatellar branch of the saphenous nerve, which
may result in regional numbness, neuropathic pain, and neuroma formation, is
substantially lower compared with BPTB and hamstring tendon harvest. A study
reported that the mean area of hypoesthesia was considerably smaller after quadriceps
tendon harvest (8.7 cm2) compared with BPTB and hamstring tendon harvest (88.2 and
70.3 cm2, respectively).12

Allografts

Allografts
Allografts are obtained from cadaver specimens. Typical allografts used in sports
medicine include patellar, hamstring, quadriceps, Achilles, and tibialis anterior/posterior
tendons. A clear advantage of allografts is that they obviate the need to harvest tissue
from the patient. This results in decreased complications related to donor site morbidity,
shorter surgical time, smaller incisions, improved cosmesis, and decreased
postoperative pain, which may facilitate a quicker recovery.
However, young patients undergoing ACL reconstruction with the use of allograft have a
substantially higher risk for graft tear. Data from the Multicenter Orthopaedic Outcomes
Network Knee Group show that the risk of tear after ACL reconstruction with the use of
allografts is 5.2 times higher than the risk of tear after ACL reconstruction with the use of
BPTB autografts (odds ratio, 5.2; P < 0.01). In addition, the study showed that allograft

use in younger patients was the only predictor of a tear.13
The quality of the allograft tissue may vary depending on the tissue bank processing
method and sterilization techniques. Although different tissue banks use many
proprietary processing techniques, a common and effective method of sterilization is
gamma irradiation; however, gamma irradiation of more than 3 mrad has been shown to
weaken the graft tissue by generating free radicals, which may adversely affect collagen
structure. Pretreatment with the use of free radical scavengers, such as dimethyl
sulfoxide and propylene glycol, has been shown to mitigate the negative effects of
gamma irradiation on the biomechanical properties of the graft.14 In addition,
processing with the use of chemicals, such as ethylene oxide or peracetic acid–ethanol,
also may substantially increase the risk of graft rupture. Treatment with ethylene oxide
can increase chronic inflammatory reaction, resulting in persistent joint effusion
requiring graft removal.15 Sterilization with the use of peracetic acid–ethanol has been
shown to slow graft remodeling and reduce the biomechanical integrity of the graft
tissue compared with the use of nonsterilized allografts and autografts.16
The risk of viral or bacterial disease transmission with the use of allografts is low. To
date, three cases of viral disease transmission have been reported, including one case of
HIV infection in 1995 and two cases of hepatitis C after ACL reconstruction with the use
of BPTB allograft.17,18 The risk of HIV transmission from allograft tissue is estimated to
be 1 in 1.6 million.19,20
Allograft tissue incorporates at a slower rate compared with autografts, and an immune
response to the allograft tissue may develop. In the pediatric patient population (10 to
19 years), allografts are associated with a failure rate four times higher than that of
autografts.21 A meta-analysis of 76 studies comparing BPTB autografts and allografts for
ACL reconstruction showed that patients who underwent ACL reconstruction with the
use of an autograft had better outcomes (subjective International Knee Documentation
Committee, Lysholm Knee Scale, and Tegner scores; single-leg hop and KT-1000 tests).
Conversely, patients who underwent ACL reconstruction with the use of BPTB allograft
had better rates of return to preinjury activity level, higher overall International Knee
Documentation Committee scores, and less anterior knee pain; however, allograft BPTB
resulted in a threefold increase in graft rupture rates compared with autografts (12.7%

Scaffolds
Scaffolds typically are used to augment tendon repairs, such as patellar tendon repair, Achilles
tendon repair, superior capsule reconstruction, or rotator cuff repair augmentation with an
onlay graft. Several types of patches are available (Figure 3).
Xenografts are made from animal dermis, pericardium, or small intestine submucosa (Table
1).
Synthetic grafts are made from Artelon fibers (a knitted, degradable, polyurethane urea fabric)
or a woven poly-L-lactic acid material available in sheets.


Scaffolds
Acellular human dermal allografts have been shown to result in greater suture retention
and higher load-to-failure strength compared with xenograft or synthetic grafts.23-25
Compared with other types of scaffolds, dermal allografts have been shown to augment
tendon repair without causing stress shielding.24 Over time, biologic patches are
reabsorbed and replaced with fibrous collagenous tissue, whereas nonabsorbable
synthetic patches are isolated and covered with a thick layer of granulation tissue that
may resemble tendinous material. A recent study reported on 23 patients who
underwent large or massive rotator cuff repair augmented with the use of a bioinductive
collagen patch. At 2-year follow-up, 22 of the 23 patients (96%) had complete healing of
the rotator cuff tear as observed on MRIs and ultrasonographic images. Serial
ultrasonography demonstrated an increase in tendon thickness at 12 months
postoperatively. No complications related to the implant were reported.26
Implants
A wide variety of implants are used in sports medicine. The primary goal of implants in sports
medicine is to facilitate soft-tissue healing by anatomically reducing and holding tissue at the
approximate injury location.
Suture Anchors

Suture anchors are commonly used in many arthroscopic procedures. Early generations of
anchors were made of surgical grade metal and have been largely replaced by biodegradable
anchors.
Current anchors are radiolucent and are made from biodegradable materials, such as poly-L-
lactic acid and poly-D,L-lactic acid or nonabsorbable polyether ether ketone (PEEK).
All-suture anchors have been shown to have biomechanical properties similar to those of
metal screws and bioabsorbable, biocomposite, and PEEK anchors.
Knotless anchors have shown fixation strength comparable to that of knotted anchors.
The most common modes of failure of biodegradable anchors are eyelet breakage and anchor
pullout.
Several high-strength sutures have been developed and are commonly used in sports
medicine. These sutures are made with braided ultra-high–molecular-weight polyethylene
(UHMWPE). These nonabsorbable sutures have been shown to be superior in biomechanical
studies compared with conventional braided polyester sutures.27
Suture Anchor Materials

Suture Anchor Materials
Suture anchors play a pivotal role in arthroscopic procedures. Historically, suture
anchors were made of surgical-grade metal. Complications associated with these
anchors included loosening, migration, incarceration within the joint space resulting in
chondral damage, and interference with imaging studies such as MRI. In the past 20
years, biodegradable anchors have been developed and currently are widely used by
orthopaedic surgeons. Current anchors are radiolucent and are made from
biodegradable materials, such as poly-L-lactic acid and poly-D,L-lactic acid, or
nonabsorbable PEEK. Biocomposite implants combine a biodegradable polymer with a
bioceramic material to degrade more rapidly and encourage osteoconductive ingrowth.
Bioceramic materials include beta-tricalcium phosphate (most commonly used), calcium
hydroxyapatite, calcium sulfate, and calcium carbonate (Figure 4).

Biochemical Considerations

Biochemical Considerations
The ideal suture anchor should have a high pullout strength to coapt soft-tissue to bone
and should be biologically compatible with local soft-tissue and bone to prevent an
inflammatory reaction, which would compromise the healing process. In addition, the
timeline for degradation of the implant must allow sufficient time for soft-tissue healing.
Basic suture anchor design consists of an anchor body with a distal eyelet containing one
or more UHMWPE sutures.

Suture-based anchors or all-suture anchors are made entirely of suture material. The
anchor portion is a sleeve or tape made from a suture material through which one or
more UHMWPE-based sutures are woven or passed (Figure 5). After it is inserted into
bone, pulling on the suture limbs will cinch the sleeve or tape against the overlying
cortical bone, creating a ball, which serves as the fixation point.
Figure 5 Photograph shows Q-Fix all-suture anchors (Smith & Nephew). (Courtesy of
Smith & Nephew, Andover, MA.)
All-suture anchors have been shown to have biomechanical properties similar to those
of metal screws and those of bioabsorbable, biocomposite, and PEEK anchors. The
density of the cortical bone appears to be the main determinant of the initial fixation
strength of these anchors.28 The ultimate failure load of an all-suture anchor correlates
with the number of sutures. For example, the ultimate failure strength of a triple-loaded
all-suture anchor is 564 N, which is considerably higher than that of double-loaded
anchors (465 N) and single-loaded anchors (256 N).29 A systematic review found that all-
suture anchors have biomechanical properties similar to or better than those of regular
anchors.28 A recent study showed that all-suture anchors had greater load to 2-mm
displacement with cyclic loading and ultimate load to failure compared with PEEK
anchors.30 Another biomechanical study evaluated all-suture anchors versus titanium
anchors in proximal hamstring repairs. The study showed considerably higher load to
failure for all-suture anchors compared with titanium anchors (799 N versus 573 N); no
substantial difference in displacement was noted between the two types of
anchors.31 Screw-in suture anchors with fully threaded constructs allow for

simultaneous fixation in the cortical and cancellous bone and typically are stronger than
punch-in anchors.
Knotless anchors have shown fixation strength comparable to that of knotted
anchors.32 A recent study involving 34 orthopaedic surgeons evaluated the
biomechanical properties of knotted and knotless fixation and evaluated the variability
of these fixation methods. The mean load to displacement and load to failure were
considerably greater with knotless fixation with suture tape (199 N) compared with
knotted (59 N) and knotless fixation with No. 2 suture (90 N). In addition, although no
substantial difference was found in load to failure of knotless and knotted fixation with
No. 2 suture, the mean load to displacement was considerably greater with the knotless
fixation. In addition, the knotted group demonstrated considerably greater variability in
load to failure compared with the knotless group. For comparison, the maximum force
generated across a 4-cm rotator cuff tear is approximately 302 N. Repair with the use of
two double-loaded anchors results in six fixation points and 50 N per fixation point.
Therefore, any fixation construct should exceed this minimum force (50 N).33,34
The size and placement of the implant in the cortical and cancellous bone determine
fixation strength. Subcortical placement of the anchor achieves greater strength than
burying the implant deep into the cancellous bone. With cyclic loading, a deeply buried
anchor will migrate through the cancellous bone to the cortical surface, resulting in
displacement of the repair construct. In addition, sutures from a deep anchor can cut
through the bone, or the suture itself may fail because of excess abrasion with the
cortical bone. Larger and fully threaded anchors, such as those used in rotator cuff
repair, have a higher load-to-failure strength compared with smaller punch-in anchors
(glenoid anchors).32
The most common modes of failure of biodegradable anchors are eyelet breakage and
anchor pullout. Immediate failure may result from improper insertion of the anchor,
such as extraosseous placement of the anchor, resulting in articular cartilage damage or
anchor breakage if the anchor is impacted at a divergent angle relative to the drilled
hole. Late failure may be to the result of deep placement of the anchor, resulting in
anchor migration, or may be the result of inflammatory reaction, resulting in osteolysis,
synovitis, or cyst formation.35

Meniscal Repair Devices
Multiple meniscal repair devices exist, with no particular device offering a clear advantage over
another.
Biomechanical studies have shown that vertical mattress sutures are stronger then horizonal
mattress sutures.
All-inside meniscal repair devices consist of a UHMWPE-based suture attached to a
nonabsorbable PEEK anchor or suture-based anchor connected to a sliding self-locking knot.
Several systematic reviews reported no difference in clinical outcomes, failure rates, or
complication rates between all-inside repair and outside-in repair.

Meniscal Repair Devices
All-inside meniscal repair devices consist of a UHMWPE-based suture attached to a
nonabsorbable PEEK anchor or suture-based anchor connected with the use of a sliding
self-locking knot. These devices are passed through the meniscal fragment in a mattress
configuration. The anchor is deployed extra-articularly through the capsule, and sutures
are tensioned through the sliding, self-locking knot. Biomechanical studies have shown
that vertical mattress sutures are stronger than horizontal mattress sutures in meniscal
repairs.36
Several systematic reviews found no difference in clinical outcomes, failure, or
complication rates between all-inside and outside-in repairs.37-42 A systematic review of
six biomechanical studies found that, although all-inside repairs resulted in higher
stiffness compared with inside-out repairs, no difference in load to failure was observed
between the two repair techniques.43 A meta-analysis of 13 studies found similar failure
rates 5 years after open, outside-in, inside-out, and all-inside repair techniques.44
Inside-out repairs are associated with a higher incidence of neurapraxia or nerve
irritation, whereas all-inside repairs are associated with a higher incidence of implant

All-suture construct with no implant. Dual-pronged delivery device

Interference Screws
Interference screws are made of metal or bioabsorbable materials and achieve fixation by
engaging the bone or tendon with screw threads and compressing the graft against the bone.
Interference screws are commonly used in ACL and posterior cruciate ligament reconstruction.
Tendon pullout is the most common mode of failure after interference screw fixation.

Interference Screws
Interference screws are commonly used in ACL and posterior cruciate ligament
reconstruction, proximal biceps tenodesis, distal biceps repair, and lateral ankle
ligament reconstruction. Interference screws are made of metal or bioabsorbable
materials and achieve fixation by engaging the bone or tendon with screw threads and
compressing the graft against the bone (Figure 7). Fixation strength depends on the
screw’s material properties, core diameter, thread pitch and height, length, placement,
and insertion torque as well as the patient’s bone density. Interference screws should be
placed colinearly with the tendon because divergent placement may damage the tendon
and reduce fixation strength. The most common mode of failure after interference screw
fixation is tendon pullout. Other modes of failure include graft slippage, laceration of the
graft with screw threads, and fatigue fractures.45,46

Cortical Buttons
Cortical buttons are commonly used in distal biceps tendon repair, proximal biceps tenodesis,
ACL reconstruction, pectoralis tendon repair, and acromioclavicular reconstruction (Figure 8).
Cortical metal buttons achieve fixation through suspension against the periosteal or endosteal
cortical surface.
Common modes of failure include buttons pulling through the bone, implant migration, and
the suture loop tearing through the tendon.

Cortical Buttons
The two common types of cortical buttons are fixed-loop and newer-generation
adjustable-loop suspension devices. With first-generation fixed-loop cortical buttons, the
graft is attached to the button via a fixed-length continuous loop, which requires drilling
to a specific depth and a tunnel that is longer than the desired graft insertion length to
allow the button to flip. Conversely, with the newer adjustable-loop cortical buttons, the
graft is attached to the button via an adjustable loop that can be sequentially tightened
to pull the graft into the tunnel, thereby eliminating the need for a longer tunnel to flip
the button. In addition, the adjustable loop allows for re-tensioning of the graft after
fixation and eliminates the need to account for the length of the implant
intraoperatively.47 The ability to adjust the loop size may be particularly useful if graft-
tunnel mismatch occurs during ACL reconstruction.
Suspensory fixation with the use of cortical buttons results in a fixation point at the
cortex of the femur or tibia, which is a greater distance from the native insertion site of

the graft within the tunnel in a horizontal plane, which may lead to greater tunnel
expansion. This phenomenon is known as the windshield-wiper effect.48 In addition,
over time, graft tissue and sutures can undergo elongation because of creep, resulting in
longitudinal motion within the tunnel, contributing to greater tunnel expansion. This
phenomenon is known as the bungee-cord effect. Tunnel widening results in excessive
shearing forces, which may inhibit biologic incorporation of the graft. In addition,
subsequent widening and bone loss may complicate revision surgery if necessary.
Transfixation Pins
Transfixation pins are used for femoral tunnel fixation during ACL reconstruction.
Fixation is achieved with the use of a pin that traverses the bone tunnel by penetrating
through a four-strand graft or folding a two-strand graft to establish a quadrupled graft.
Common modes of failure of transfixation pins include cross-pin breakage, graft slippage, or
tearing. Progressive deformation of the pin may result in residual displacement over time.

Transfixation Pins
Breakage of cross-pin fixation has been reported in numerous studies, with resultant
complications, such as pin migration, protrusion, chondral injury, and iliotibial band
friction syndrome. At a mean follow-up of 26 months, a study found fractured cross pins
in 17% of patients, breach of the posterior femoral cortex in 28% of patients, and
migration of the fractured pin in 6% of patients.49 In addition, studies have reported a
higher risk of iatrogenic chondral damage if this fixation system is used through the
anteromedial portal, compared with the transtibial technique.50
